Data 360 Inspector

All-in-one toolkit for Salesforce Data Cloud — explore data, export segment rules & transforms, query any object to CSV. Read-only, zero setup.

● Read-only · nothing leaves your browser
🔍 Data 360 Inspector ↖ Drag me to your bookmarks bar
❓How to install & use
1. Show your bookmarks bar — ⌘⇧B (Mac) / Ctrl⇧B (Windows).
2. Drag the Data 360 Inspector button above onto the bookmarks bar. No install, no permissions.
3. On any Data Cloud / Data 360 page, click the bookmark — a purple circle button appears bottom-right; click it for the menu.
4. Click the bookmark again anytime to remove the tool. It never overlaps the Salesforce nav.

What it does

Works on these pages (the launcher shows only that page’s buttons) — click a row to see what you can do. All read-only.

🔁DLO → DMO Mapping CanvasAPI TooltipPin API namesExport

The mapping canvas normally shows only field labels — not the API names you actually need when building queries, transforms, or integrations. This fills that gap.

  • API Tooltip — hover a field to see its API name on both the source (DLO) and target (DMO) side; press C to copy. When on, the button shows a green “• ON” so you know it’s live.
  • Pin API names — show every API name on the canvas at once, so you can read the whole mapping without hovering. Click any pinned name to copy it (it flashes “✓ Copied”).
  • Export — download the full mapping table (source field → target field, with both API names) to Google Sheets or CSV. You can filter to a single DMO first.
Good to know: if the same label is used on both a DLO and a DMO, the tooltip marks which side it read so you’re never shown the wrong API name.
🌐Data Stream & DLOExport Fields

On a Data Stream or Data Lake Object page, export the complete field list in one click — no copy-pasting row by row.

Each row includes the API name, label, data type, status, and key qualifier (primary key / event time / etc.). Copy it straight into Google Sheets, or download as a CSV.

🗂DMO DetailExport Fields

On a Data Model Object detail page, grab both tabs of information:

  • Fields — API name, data type, whether the field is mapped, and its key qualifier.
  • Relationships — the objects this DMO is related to and the fields that join them.

Copy it into Google Sheets, or download as an Excel (XLS) file.

🗺️Data Model (ERD)Diagram

On the Data Model graph page, build a shareable entity-relationship diagram of your objects and how they connect — without drawing it by hand.

  • Generates a copyable Mermaid diagram you can paste into Lucidchart, draw.io, GitHub, or any Markdown doc.
  • Includes a cardinality legend (one-to-many, etc.) so the relationships are easy to read.
  • Searchable entity cards let you look up any object and see everything it’s connected to.
🕸️Data GraphField API NamesFiltersCopy

The Data Graph builder shows only friendly labels for the fields you pick — not the API names you need for queries and integrations. Turn on API names from the ◎ button (bottom-right) to reveal them.

  • Objects & fields — the API name appears under each object on the left and under each field on the right. It refreshes automatically as you click between objects.
  • Filters tab — the field chosen in each Sort and Condition dropdown is labelled with its API name too (and on hover).
  • Click any API name to copy it (it flashes “✓ Copied”). Every field also shows its API name on hover as a fallback.
Duplicate labels handled safely: when two fields share a label, the tool scopes to the object you’re on so you get that object’s field — and if a single object genuinely has two fields with the same label, it shows both candidates with a “(?)” marker rather than guessing.
📂Object lists (records)Open in New Tab

On any Data Cloud object list — Data Streams, Data Lake Objects, Data Model Objects, Calculated Insights, Segments, Activations, Data Graphs, Identity Resolution, and the rest — hover a row and a ⧉ button appears by its name to open that record in a new tab.

Why this helps: many of these list rows aren’t real links (the name runs a script instead of a URL), so a normal right-click → “Open in new tab” doesn’t work — today you have to duplicate the tab. The tool reads the row’s own record id and opens the exact record directly — and deliberately ignores lookup columns (e.g. a “Data Space” cell), so it always opens the row’s record, never a related one.
🧭Left & Top NavOpen in New Tab

Hover any Data Cloud navigation item — in the left side menu or the top bar — and a ⧉ button lets you open it in a new tab. Covers every item, including newer ones (Segments, Activations, Calculated Insights, AI Models, Clean Rooms, Data Shares, Semantic Layer, …).

Only real menu items get the button — ordinary record or user links on a page won’t be mistaken for navigation. You don’t need to re-click the bookmark as you move between pages.
🏁SegmentExport RulesAPI NamesContainer Path

Read and export the real logic behind a segment — API names and all — which the builder normally hides behind friendly labels.

  • Hover any attribute or rule to see its object and field API name. Press C to copy it.
  • Container Path is shown exactly as it appears when a related object’s edit panel is open — so you can see which related record a rule actually points at.
  • Export every condition — Include, Exclude, and Rank & Limit — with the full AND/OR logic, nested segments, and sub-filters preserved, plus columns for the object and field API names. Save to Google Sheets, or as HTML / Excel.
Reads only what’s on screen: the Container Path is copied straight from the open panel, never reconstructed or guessed — if it isn’t shown in Data Cloud, the tool won’t invent it.
🎯ActivationAPI NamesExport

The same help as Segment, for the activation wizard.

  • Hover any attribute in the main table or in “Add Additional Attributes” to see its object and field API name.
  • Export the activation’s included attributes, with their object and field API names, in one click.
API-name help appears on the wizard (where you’re choosing attributes). On a finished activation’s read-only detail page there are no attributes to label, so only Export is offered there.
📊Data ExplorerColumnsExport CSV

Salesforce’s Data Explorer only shows about 10 columns at a time and a limited set of rows. This lets you see and take the whole picture.

  • Columns — pick exactly which fields to show (well past the 10-column limit), reorder them, and save the set so it’s there next time. Then view all their data together in one table.
  • Sort, multi-filter, and a live row count on the results, plus an Edit SQL option if you want to tweak the query behind the view.
  • Export CSV — download the rows. Large exports fetch in batches automatically, up to 500,000 rows, and you can cancel partway.
Column choices are saved only in your own browser (per org, cleared after 90 days). Nothing is written back to Salesforce.
🔎Query EditorCountFetch & ExportExport ALLHelpful QueriesViewDownload

The Query Editor shows query results on screen, but only about 1,000 rows, and getting the full result out as a file is awkward. This adds a small toolbar (a round button, bottom-left) that does the rest. Highlight a query first to run just that one; otherwise it uses the whole editor.

What each button does:

  • # Count Gives you the exact number of rows a query returns — without downloading any data. One quick call. Works for plain queries as well as GROUP BY and JOINs.
  • ▶ Fetch & Export Fetches the rows and saves them as a CSV file. It pulls in batches behind the scenes, so it keeps going past the 1,000 on-screen rows. If your query has no LIMIT, it stops at 50,000 rows by default (and tells you there were more) — add your own LIMIT to go higher, up to 500,000. For bigger than that, use Export ALL.
  • ⤓ Export ALL Exports the entire result to a CSV, with no row cap. You pick where to save first, then the rows write straight to that file as they’re fetched — so even a very large table won’t run your browser out of memory. You can Cancel anytime, and a progress count keeps you posted. If you close the little panel while it runs, it keeps going; re-open it (or click the button again) and your progress comes right back.
  • 🔧 Helpful Queries Builds common checks for you — find duplicates, empty (null) values, stale records, orphaned keys, records in a date range, and more — just by picking an object and a column. No SQL to write. It runs through the same Count / Fetch buttons.
  • 👁 View Results Shows the fetched rows in a table right on the page (up to 2,000 rows) so you can glance at them without opening a file. Click any cell to copy it. No extra query.
  • ⬇ Download CSV Saves rows you’ve already fetched to a CSV. No new query, so no extra credits.
About Data Cloud credits: Count and Fetch each run a real query, and Data Cloud bills by rows processed (scanned), not rows returned — so a heavy JOIN or GROUP BY can cost more than its row count suggests. The toolbar shows your org’s rate and an estimate, and it remembers results — re-running the same query or re-downloading an already-fetched file is free. If you re-run an Export ALL you already did, it warns you first so you don’t pay twice.Opening very large files: a CSV can hold any number of rows, but Excel stops showing rows after about 1,048,576 and Google Sheets after about 10 million cells (so fewer rows the more columns you have). If an export is bigger, the tool tells you, and suggests Power Query or a database so you don’t silently lose data.A note on huge tables (tens of millions of rows): a browser isn’t the right tool for a full dump at that scale — it’s slow, uses a lot of credits, and the file is hard to open. For those, export in slices (for example by date range) or use a server-side option like the Data Cloud Query API or a data share. This toolbar is ideal for counts, exploring, and exports up to a few hundred thousand (and into the low millions with Export ALL).
⚙️Data TransformView Definition

Understand what a Data Transform actually does without reading its raw definition.

The tool reads the transform automatically and writes a plain-English, step-by-step summary: the sources it reads, the filters it applies, any formulas and joins, the outputs it writes, and which fields are kept, dropped, or renamed along the way.

Download the summary as an HTML file (which you can print to PDF). An optional AI explanation is available if you want it rewritten in even simpler terms.

Modals are draggable & resizable. The × on a menu just closes it; to remove the tool entirely, click the bookmark again.

🔒Privacy & safety
  • Runs entirely in your browser — no external servers, no third-party services.
  • Uses Salesforce’s own APIs (same-origin). No data leaves your browser or your org.
  • Nothing is stored permanently — the tool disappears on page reload. Column selections use localStorage (per-org, 90-day TTL).
  • Read-only: it never creates, modifies, or deletes any Salesforce data.
  • No installation required — no package, no Connected App, no admin approval.
